    URL: https://developer.mozilla.org/fr/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Unary_negation
    Published: 2025-02-17T00:00:00.000Z
    SUMMARY: The unary negation operator (`-`) in JavaScript is used to convert its operand into its negative equivalent. For example, if you apply the unary negation to a positive number like `4`, it will return `-4`. This operator can also convert non-numeric values into numbers; for instance, applying it to the string `"4"` will also yield `-4`. 

Here are some examples:
- For a variable `const x = 4;`, using `const y = -x;` results in `y` being `-4`.
- For a string `const a = "4";`, using `const b = -a;` results in `b` being `-4`.

The unary negation operator is widely supported across all browsers since July 2015. For further details, you can refer to the [MDN documentation](https://developer.mozilla.org/fr/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Unary_negation).
    HIGHLIGHTS:
